label: Synthesized Legalist statecraft combining law (fa), administrative art (shu), and positional power (shi)
description: Han Feizi unified the competing strands of Legalism into a comprehensive science of autocratic government, combining Shang Yang's public penal law (fa), Shen Buhai's bureaucratic statecraft (shu), and Shen Dao's circumstantial power (shi).
historicalContext: Composed in the State of Han on the eve of the Qin unification of China in 221 BCE.
dialecticalTension: Displaces the rule of virtuous men (renzhi) with the objective rule of institutional law and administrative mechanics (fazhi).

citations.author: Han Feizi
citations.quote: Law is what is codified in books and proclaimed to the people; statecraft is what is harbored in the ruler's breast to control his ministers secretly.

citations.author: Yuri Pines
citations.work: Envisioning Eternal Empire: Chinese Political Thought of the Warring States Era

label: Synthesized Daoist non-action (wu-wei) into the ruler's detached institutional posture
description: Han Feizi wrote the earliest surviving commentaries on the Daodejing (the Jie Lao and Yu Lao chapters), adapting Laozi's metaphysical wu-wei into the ultimate administrative strategy: the ruler remains inscrutable, allowing the machinery of law to execute itself.
historicalContext: The synthesis of Huang-Lao Daoist metaphysics with Legalist institutional governance in pre-Qin China.
dialecticalTension: Transmutes Daoist natural quietude into an instrument of imperial state surveillance and total administrative control.

citations.author: Han Feizi
citations.quote: The Dao abides in non-assertion, yet nothing remains unaccomplished... The enlightened ruler rests in non-action above, while ministers toil in action below.

citations.author: Sarah A. Queen
citations.sectionOrPage: Dao Companion to the Philosophy of Han Feizi, pp. 197–232

label: Parallel formulation of cold political realism, institutional law, and statecraft
description: Comparative political philosophers highlight the striking parallel between Han Feizi and Niccolò Machiavelli: both stripped politics of moral sentimentalism, analyzing power through fear, objective institutional incentives, and human self-interest.
historicalContext: The trans-epochal resonance between ancient Chinese Legalism and early modern Italian Renaissance political theory.
dialecticalTension: Han Feizi constructed an impersonal bureaucratic legal order independent of individual genius, whereas Machiavelli retained a focus on virtù and republican contingency.

citations.author: Han Feizi
citations.quote: The ruler does not value being loved by his subjects, but being feared by them.

citations.author: Arthur Waley
citations.work: Three Ways of Thought in Ancient China
